Mr. Speaker, I wish to

Canadians in London are asking to-day why Canada alone among the dominions, and almost alone among all the countries o>f the world, is not represented at the Parliamentary International Conference on Commerce.
All the great nations are represented there, and even countries like Afghanistan, Portugal, Luxemburg, Turkey, Honduras and San Salvador have their parliamentary or diplomatic representation. Australia has sent three delegates; New Zealand three, of whom Sir Thomas McKenzie, is one; South Africa one; and the Indias ithree. But Canada has no one.
The reason given, in reply to questions put on the subject, is that Canada has nobody here who ds able to represent the country officially. The Hon. E. jST. Rhodes, Premier of Nova Scotia, ought to be the official delegate of Canada, but he sailed yesterday on the steamship Arabic to return home, and apparently there is nobody who .is able ,to take his place.
The first sitting of the conference is being held to-day at Westminster /paiace. It is proposed to discuss all questions relative to international companies, to bankruptcy, to agricultural credits and problems of urgency. The object is to elaborate plans capable of guiding countries which contemplate instituting a code of commerce.
I should like to ask the government if they can give us any information whether Canada is really represented or to be represented; and if not, why not?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the despatch read by my right hon. friend it sounded to me as though it was a well-intentioned bit of publicity for Mr. Rhodes. This I do not take exception to.

As to capable representation, there can be

Sumas Landowners

Was Canada invited to have a representative at the Geneva Conference on Disarmament ? Was Canada consulted as >to policy, and has the British representative, the Chancellor of .the Duchy of Lancaster, been instructed to speak for Canada ?
In answer I would say that the Conference on Disarmament has not yet been held. In September 1925 the assembly of the League of Nations requested the council to make preliminary studies with a view to holding a conference for the reduction and limitation of armaments. In December the council appointed a preparatory commission consisting of representatives named by each of the ten members of the council and by certain other members of the leauge specially interested by reason of their geographical position, namely, Poland, Jugoslavia, Rumania, Finland, Holland and Bulgaria. Invitations were also extended to three non-members of the League, the United States, Germany and Russia, and accepted by the first two. The meeting which is being held at Geneva in the present week is simply a meeting of this preparatory commission, on which Canada and the great majority of the other members of the league are not directly represented. The Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, who is a member of the preparatory commission, represents the government of Great Britain, and has not received any instructions to speak for Canada. If it is found feasible to hold a disarmament conference in 1927, as is now anticipated, Canada, and all other members of the league, will doubtless be represented and our country will have an opportunity of setting forth its views.
Perhaps the Prime Minister would tell us what Canada has to disarm.

The question to which my hon. friend refers now was answered in part, and I will undertake to see that a supplementary answer is tabled giving my hon. friend the information he wishes.

I wish to make an appeal to the Minister of Finance in connection with the exemptions for dependent children. I have a letter here from a constituent in Mount Royal in the course of which he says:
I have a daughter who is over twenty years of age, who, unfortunately, cannot earn her own living on account of having the use of only the left hand from birth. I have to look after her, and I am not exempt for the $500 on her account.
It does seem to me that in a case of that kind where a child is incapacitated from birth from earning a living, the age for exemption should not be limited to eighteen years, but should be indefinite. It may be that in cases of that kind, if an appeal is made to the Minister of Finance, the exemption will apply only in the oase of parents whose income is not in excess of, say, six or eight thousand dollars. But there is a germ of a fair case, it seems to me, in the circumstances I have referred to, and I would ask the minister if he would be good enough to give it his consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my colleague the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) has to do with the administration of the act and as he has given much time to the preparation of the measure now before the House, and understands the new regulations very much better than I do, I am going to ask him to answer any questions that are submitted to him by hon. gentlemen.

In answer to my hon. friend from Mount Royal, I might say that the question which he has just submitted was very seriously considered, but it has been found practically impossible to give any additional exemptions to a married person on account of dependent children over the age of eighteen years. If an exemption were made for a case like that mentioned by my hon. friend, it would give rise to such a number of false claims which it would be impossible for the Commissioner of Taxation and the inspectors of taxation to investigate and approve that it was felt that in spite of the fact that in occasional cases there must be severe hardship, it would be better to adhere strictly to the rule making the age limit eighteen years. I would point out, however, that in the case of unmarried persons who have dependents who are relatives, to a certain degree, and in the case of widows and widowers having dependent children over
eighteen years of age, the fact that they are obliged to support these dependents is taken into consideration in the act and they are placed in the same class as married persons, that is to say, they have an exemption of $3,000 instead" of $1,500. It has been found impossible, however, to draw the line and define in an absolute way any exemption which could be granted to married persons having dependent children over eighteen years of age.

How does the age limit in this case compare with the age in the case of fixing allowances for widows of soldiers? The amount of pension payable in that case depends to a certain extent upon the number of children under a certain age. Is the age limit in that case eighteen years, the same as in this?
I am not familiar with the terms of the Pensions Act. I remember very well when the act was discussed in the House, but I cannot recall the exact age that it provides.
Eighteen years.
Of course, in so far as pensions received under the Pensions Act are concerned, they are exempted entirely from taxation under this act.
May I draw the minister's attention to the fact that the age is not limited to eighteen if the child is attending school continually.

My hon. friend is referring, of course, to the Pensions Act. That request was very strongly urged upon the government by the hon. member for Labelle, who pointed out that the age limit of children should be increased owing to the fact that a large number of parents kept their children in schools and colleges long after they had passed the age of eighteen, and that that was the very time in life when they were the greatest expense to their parents. There is a lot to be said in favour of that argument.
May I just draw the Minister's attention to the fact that in some of the provinces the parents are forced to keep the child in school up to a certain age, but not after eighteen?

Yes, there may be some
provinces where a system of compulsory education exists, but in no case does the age exceed eighteen years.
Mr. EULiER: Has the minister considered the advisability of including amongst the ex-
Income War Tax Act

emptions one that is not there now? I refer to the case of children who are beyond the adult age, have become permanent invalids, and are a charge upon their parents, perhaps a heavier charge than those who are not of adult age. It seems to me there should be an exemption in such cases.

The same answer would
apply to my hon. friend's question as to the question asked by my hon. friend from Mount Royal. There are very many meritorious cases where such an exemption should be granted, but it is so terribly difficult to control these cases and prevent fraud that the officers of the department claim it is absolutely impossible to provide for an exemption.

Would the minister make
a succinct statement in regard to the respective classes dealt with? Then we should be in a position to deal with the matter intelligently.

I think the time is opportune to urge upon the Minister of Finance that the exemption of $3,000 be raised to $5,000. In the city from which I come there are many w'orking people whose earnings amount to $3,000 and they have to pay a double headed tax. They have to pay a tax on May 1,' in full to the municipality and a tax to the federal authorities on the same date. So the first instalment of the municipal tax falls due on May 1, and the federal tax is payable about the same time. Possibly the payment of the federal tax might be deferred until a later period in the year as the double header tax is a hardship. Then as to the forms. They are so worded that it takes a Philadelphia lawyer to construe them properly and fill them out correctly. In my opinion the taxation forms could be greatly simplified like municipal taxation forms. There is another point to which I wish to draw attention. This tax was originally imposed as a temporary war measure. In the United States the exemption has been raised, I think, up to about $7,500. In Australia it has also been raised. Here it still remains at $3,000. The ability of the people to pay income tax on that amount has been greatly lessened by the decline in the value of the dollar. The Minister of Finance, a year ago said he would have a conference with the provincial and municipal authorities on the subject of taxation, seek to avoid double header methods and secure co-ordination. May I remind him that the municipalities, unlike the federal government, do not have an unlimited source of taxation. And yet there are enormous

responsibilities placed upon them by the federal and provincial governments that do not properly come within their sphere.
In the province of Ontario, for example, the municipalities are required to maintain the registry offices, the gaols, the courthouses, and many other institutions, which should be obligations of the provincial government, more especially in view of the fact that the provinces receive a Dominion subsidy, under the British North America Act, for many of these purposes. In other provinces there are also burdens imposed of a similar nature. Had I been in a position to do so in 1917, I would have carried the question of the right to impose this income tax-which is distinctly a war measure-to the Privy Council. I had at the time the authority of five or six leading counsel in the Toronto district for the statement that this tax, which was levied as a war measure, was disinctly ultra vires of the federal parliament. It affects property and civil rights, a matter entirely within the purview of the provinces. It is too bad that the working classes of Canada should be subjected to this tax the legality of which is doubtful to say the least. This tax properly comes within the category of a "nuisance" tax. It bears with special severity upon those people who, although they earn $3,000, find it hard enough to live at present with everything at such a high cost. The worst feature of the matter is that many people in receipt of large incomes escape the payment of 4 p.m. income tax altogether. They go over to England and are not subject to income there because they say their domicile is in Canada. In Canada they escape because they say they are domiciled in England, with the result that they escape in Canada and England as well. I know of three prominent Canadian citizens who are in receipt of an income of at least a million dollars and yet do not pay a cent of income tax in England or Canada. I should like to see this matter taken up on this side of the House. It should be dealt with by the "board of strategy. I do not know what has become of our board of strategy; I wish it would wake up and do something for the working classes. The Trades and Labour Council of Toronto have protested against this unjust taxation over and over again. I am sorry that more representatives of the working men in this House do not rise and protest against the double header tax. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and his colleague, the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) are supposed to represent the working classes here, and why they

Income War Tax Act
do not take a firm stand on this question I do not know. I do not see them here to help the workingman get his just due. What about the so-called independent hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa)? He is supposed to be an Independent; he has no board of strategy over him to tell him what to do. Where does he stand in regard to this matter?
I want to protest on behalf of the working classes of the city from which I come against this particular tax, the form of tax, the method of collecting it on the very same day as the municipal tax, and the method of sending a bailiff or a federal officer to summon members of the working classes to the police court for non-payment. Many workingmen were summoned before His Honour Judge Cohen in Toronto to compel them to pay $5.47 in taxes. These men are, many of them, returned soldiers with children, and they are out of work. This tax is collected on the 1925 income and many of these men who had work in 1925 have gone to the United States or are out of work in 1926 and have not the means of paying this tax. There are other men in Christie street hospital to-day who in 1925 had jobs and are now taxed though out of work.
The present Minister of Labour (Mir. Elliott) has left the chamber. The former Minister of Labour said that he was a friend of the working classes of Toronto. Where does the Labour Minister stand in this particular matter and where does the government stand? The government was supposed to go after the big interests; they said that we were the party of the big interests. I serve no big interests in this country. I have suffered in the battle against the big interests and I am prepared to suffer again. Yet these same big interests are escaping their share of the taxes to-day. The Mail and Empire and the Toronto Star talk about taxes and the working classes. There are no two greater enemies of the Conservative party and the working classes than the Michigan-controlled Toronto Star and the Montreal-owned Mail and Empire, the biggest load the Liberal-Conservative party are carrying to-day in Ontario.
I am here pleading for $5,000 exemption for the under-dog. There are 30,000 men out of work in our city and I appeal to the Minister of Customs and Excise, who is a young minister, and to the Minister of Finance, who is not unfriendly to the working classes-the under-dog who has to pay this double-header income tax-to raise this exemption to $5,000. They should also restore to the municipalities their former exclusive privilege of collecting income tax which, under the British North
America Act, has been the field of the municipalities from confedration to 1917, when the Union government, which I voted for but never supported and never would support, brought it in only as a war measure. The minister should now restore this tax to the municipalities to whom it belongs, and not invade a field of taxation that does not belong to them. Little or no revenue will come out of the $5,000 men; why not increase the exemption to that extent?

The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked me to point out the dependents provided for in the act giving the taxpayer the additional exemption or the same exemption as married persons. There is no change in that; it is the same as in the present act. The exemption of $3,000, which was formerly $2,000, is given in the case of a married person, in the case of any person who has depending upon him a parent or grandparent, a daughter, or a sister, a son or brother under twenty-one years of age, or a son or brother of any age incapable of self support on account of mental or physical infirmity. Those are the exemptions which enable a person who is not married or who is a widow or widower to get the same exemption as the married man.
Why does the case which I cited not come under the clause which the minister just quoted? It is apparently included there.

I understood my hon. friend to make the request that responsibility for a child over eighteen years of age, but owing to physical infirmity dependent upon his parents, should entitle the parent to have the same exemption as if the child was under eighteen years of age.
The minister read something that seems to include it.

That is the case to which the hon. member for Mount Royal referred and it is a typical case of which examples have come before many of us. That case appeals very strongly to me and it ought to appeal very strongly to the government. The difficulties to which the minister has referred in dealing with cases and eliminating frauds have perhaps been exaggerated in hi3 mind. I can imagine that people might attempt to put up a fraudulent claim such as the minister suggested, but such cases ought to be capable of demonstration. In the case of a man with a daughter who is an invalid over eighteen years of age, a certificate of a physician of good standing should be prima facie evidence and the taxpayer ought to receive
Income War Tax Act

consideration. I have no doubt regulations could be framed which would meet the situation and do justice. I think at present injustice is done.

What was the purpose in the first place of fixing an age limit of eighteen? I presume it was assumed that when a child reached eighteen years it had reached an age when it could look after itself and that up to eighteen years it was dependent upon its parents. If that was the assumption and if that is the reason why the age was fixed at eighteen, then the child who is physically defective and who may be twenty-five or twenty-six or thirty years of age is still a child and still dependent notwithstanding the fact that it has passed1 the age of eighteen. If it is reasonable to give the parent exemption for a child up to the age of eighteen years on the assumption that it is not able to take care of itself up to that age, if we want to be logical we should extend that in the case of children who have physical defects or infirmities which prevent them from earning t'heir own living and keep them as a continual charge upon their parents. The minister will 'be well advised to incorporate that in this bill. If there is any case where the parent needs help it is in that of children who are suffering from infirmities which make them a charge perhaps for life upon their parents.
In fixing the age limit we should endeavour to aim at uniformity. There is an age limit in connection with military pensions; a widow receives a certain amount and so much for each child up to a certain age, and when the child reaches that age the pension is correspondingly lessened. I presume the assumption is that up to that age the child is not able to look after itself and must depend upon the parents. It seems hardly reasonable that we should fix in the one case a different age limit from that in the other. 'Let us have something like uniformity in the matter. I understood the minister to say that vdien there were dependents the age limit for exemption was twenty-one years.

That applied merely to the son or brother. It marks the difference between the son or brother and the daughter or sister-the daughter or sister at any age and the son or brother under twenty-one, unless he is an invalid unable to support himself.

I do not see why there should be any difference there. If the age limit for dependents is fixed at eighteen years in one case, why should it not be left at eighteen years all through so that it would

be uniform? I do want to associate myself with hon. gentlemen who have appealed to the minister on behalf of those persons who, because of physical infirmities, remain children regardless of their age. Consideration should be given them.

As I heard the minister cite the section of the act it seemed to include all children, irrespective of age, if they were dependent on their parents. I am not clear on that point. There is a very grave injustice worked to a great many people, I know of many instances in which persons of over eighteen, indeed, persons of twenty and twenty-five, are entirely incapacitated and the father finds it a very real hardship to support such dependents without some allowance in respect of his income tax. Such a parent should receive the exemption, for in many cases it costs more to support these grown-ups than it does to keep a young ohild. While I appreciate the difficulty that may be encountered in framing the act in such a way as to obviate any possibility of fraud, I urge the minister at the same time to consider the justice of the case. Would the minister mind explaining in what respect the act does not cover such a case as I suggest?

The section of the act to
which I have been referring is not the one providing the exemption of $500 per child. It is that section which places the unmarried person in the same position as the married person by reason of the fact that, although, unmarried, he has dependents to care for. It increases the total exemption in that case from $1,500 to $3,000. The representations of my hon. friend from Frontenac appeal to the human instincts of every hon. member; certainly they appeal to the instincts of the Minister of Finance and of myself. The matter, however, presents serious difficulties from the standpoint of administration. To substantiate this statement I need only observe that when this act was introduced by the government supported by my hon. friend from Frontenac, this eighteen year age limit was incorporated in it without any provision for dependent "children" over that age. This was copied from United States and British legislation and, I am told, it was found by the officers of the department that in various countries where an attempt was made to provide especially for such cases as my hon. friend has in mind, it proved absolutely impossible to draw the line at such physical or mental infirmity as would render a person of greater age a charge upon his parents. In some cases a slight deafness is

Income War Tax Act
considered a physical infirmity; the blindness of one eye or the loss of one arm unfits a person in some circles for any work. Among the poorer classes, means are devised by which such persons are enabled to earn their own livelihood, and as a matter of fact they not infrequently do so quite efficiently. No doubt there are cases in which the exemption should be granted, but it is feared that there would be so much recrimination as between the really deserving case, where exemption would be perfectly justified, and the numerous cases in which the applicants might not be entitled to exemption, that the responsibility placed upon the minister would be entirely too great. My hon. friend from Frontenac, referring to the Pensions Act, points out that a certain age limit is fixed therein, the needs of the widow being considered less after the child has reached that age. I may be mistaken, but I understand that no provision is made even in the Pensions Act for children who have passed a certain age but who nevertheless are still dependent upon the widowed mother because of physical or mental infirmity.
I think you are right in that.

Has the minister considered the question of giving relief to the parents of children who are confined permanently in asylums for the insane, in which case there would be no cause for fear that fraud might be practised upon the government. I have in mind the specific case of a father whose wife and two children are permanently in the Protestant Hospital for the insane at Verdun. In a case of that kind no fraud could be perpetrated on the government as the statistics could be provided by the provincial government. In every case where a person over eighteen is confined in an insane asylum it seems to me that, on the presentation of a certificate from the institution to that effect, some relief ought to be afforded.

There is considerable merit
in the claim, but the hon. member will realize that in the case of children confined in an institution of that nature part of the fees are paid to the institution by the provincial government.

Not if the parents
can afford to pay the fees.

I know of one individual
who pays $60 a month for each of his relatives.

The parent pays in the
west if he can afford it.

I was under the impression that if the father was able to afford the fees he was obliged to pay them without any assistance from the provincial authorities, but I thought that there might have been provision for other cases. In such a case as my hon. friend suggests, fraud would appear to be impossible, but the matter will require consideration. It will be discussed with the experts of the department and inasmuch as compliance with the suggestion would mean a reduction rather than an increase in taxation, the amendment could be made in the bill without the necessity of introducing a new resolution.
Who are these illustrious experts?

I am quite willing to tell
my hon. friend. One of the experts is in the House at the present time. I refer to Mr. Breadner, who was appointed Commissioner of Taxation by the former government and who is a most excellent official. The other gentleman, who has been consulted concerning questions of this nature, is Mr. Russell. His opinion is sought in connection with all matters relating to tariff and taxation. The legal aspect of the bills has been submitted to the solicitors of the department of Customs working in the Income Tax branch under Mr. Breadner.

I was only anxious to
get the minister's opinion of Mr. Breadner on record.
You wanted it in writing.

I do not think that the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) is practical, that in the case of people confined in an insane asylum certificates could be produced for the purpose of giving concessions to their relatives. All insane cases do not go to asylums and the hon. member would experience some difficulty in putting his suggestion into practice. It might lead to further difficulty. It is clear to me that the suggestion cannot be carried out in that limited way. The insane are both in and outside asylums. It is perhaps hardly necessary to state that, but at the same time it is not possible to distinguish between disabilities, mental or otherwise,, provided they are disabilities. I think the minister will finally come to the conclusion that the matter must remain as it is.

Mr. Chairman,
during the period of the war we were dealing with separation allowances in the Militia department, we were meeting exactly the

3763	COMMONS
Income War Tax Act
same difficulties that the minister has to meet at the present time. The law then was so drastic that there was no way of dealing with special cases. Finally we had to amend the law-by order in council it is true, but under the War Measures Act that had the force of an act of parliament-and we organized in the Separation Allowance branch of the Militia department a special board. If the cases were extraordinary, power was given the minister by order in council to deal with them. I cannot see why there should not be a similar provision in the present law. Otherwise you cannot deal with these exceptions legally. During the war we had hundreds of thousands of cases, and they were all adjusted satisfactorily by means of that special legislation. I would therefore suggest that similar provision should be made in the act to enable the minister to deal with such special cases instead of referring them to the House of Commons.

It seems to me that the
suggestion of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Sir Eugene Fiset) would entail the appointment of another board, which would increase the expense of the collection of these taxes. But why could not such cases be dealt with in this way? The man or the woman responsible to make a sworn declaration as to the facts, and to be subject to severe penalties in case of fraud. It seems to me that would be a simple way of dealing with such cases without increasing the staff, for these are special cases and would not be numerous.

Mr. Chairman, do I
understand that a married man with no family is exempt from income tax up to $3,000?

A married man with no
family is exempt up to $3,000 if only one of the married couple makes an income tax return.
If the combined incomes of the husband and wife do not exceed $3,000 they are exempt?
Yes.
Do you think that is fair? Do you think that any man who is in receipt of an income of $3,000 should not help to pay some of the taxes due to the war?

I have only my wife
to take care of, but I do not feel that I should be exempt from income tax on a $3,000 income. I was one of those who gave my family to the war, but in spite of that I do not want to be exempted from payment of income tax on anything like that amount. It is too high.

Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to discuss our Dominion income tax law without having a copy of the consolidated act before one, but in the latest edition of Plax-ton and Varcoe, who I think are officials of the income tax department, I find that the allowance for dependent children was introduced first by an amending act in 1918, and was limited to children under 16 years, but was extended by an amendment in 1919 to cover children under 18 years. In the definitions to the act as at present consolidated I find that "dependent child" means:
A child under 21 years of age and dependent on his parents for support, or over 21 years of age and dependent on his parents for support on account of physical or mental incapacity.
It does seem to me that this definition might be applied to cover the suggestions made by hon. members who have preceded me. While I am on my feet I should like to ask a question with respect to another matter. Under clause 1 of the resolution it is provided:
That the amount of income exempted from the tax be increased to $3,000 in the case of a married person or householder.
Is it proposed in the act itself to define "householder"?
Yes.
So that will come up for further consideration under the bill to be presented?
Yes.
Mr. Chairman, what proportion of those now paying income tax does the minister estimate will be exempt altogether as a result of this legislation?

The officers of the department inform us that the percentage of persons now paying income tax, and who will not be called upon to pay under this legislation, is about 35 per cent. It is very difficult to estimate exactly owing to the fact, as pointed out by the right hon. leader of the opposition yesterday, that there may be a very few

Income War Tax Act
persons in the country not paying tax at the present time who will pay taxes under the amended act.

That means that approximately 150,000 of our total population will be paying income tax next year. I should like to point out to the minister that our 9,000,000 people to-day are paying very heavy taxes upon the essentials that enter into their daily life. Yesterday the minister stated that as a result of sub paragraph 4 of section 19 BBB, there is nothing entering into a poor man's budget that pays any tax at all. I should like to ask him: Since when does the poor man require no clothing, no kitchen utensils, no furniture?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I submit that my hon. friend will be quite in order in discussing this matter later when the sales tax is before the House in the form of a bill, but if we are ever going to get through the session I would suggest that we keep to the question before the committee.
The minister is justifying these reductions in taxation by stating that the sales tax has been removed from the necessities of the poor man.	.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. We are dealing with the income tax.

Mr. Chairman, let me speak to the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance. In dealing with the section of the *Income War Tax Act now before the committee it is necessary to deal with taxation generally, because this reduction is being justified by the statement made by the Minister of Customs yesterday that all taxes have been removed from the budget of the poor man. I am now suggesting that there is no justification for the action of the government in relieving that portion of the people of Canada who can pay taxation, before the poor man and the public generally are relieved of the very onerous taxation imposed by this government. That taxation, I suggest, consists of practically everything entering into a poor man's budget; it consists of his clothing; of everything that goes to furnish his house, his kitchen utensils, his furniture and his rugs; everything except his food. Let me tell the minister that there never was a sales tax on food, with some very minor exceptions, consisting chiefly of cereals. I suggest very strongly, Mr. Chairman, that I am in order in discussing this matter and that the government has adopted the wrong principle. They are relieving from taxation a very few people, while still imposing upon the people 14011-239J
generally very onerous war taxes which, in my opinion, should be removed before the government commence to relieve that small section of the people who can afford to pay.

I have no doubt that my
hon. friend is quite well satisfied, since in discussing the point of order he has made his argument. Without going into a .discussion of the sales tax I only wish to correct his quotation from yesterday's Hansard. He said I remarked that everything required by a poor man is exempted from taxation. He should have read the full statement, and he would have found that I spoke as follows:
Everything required by a poor man, everything going into a poor man's budget and almost everything really a necessity of life, does not pay any sales tax at all.
That is worse than my statement of what the minister said, and it is not correct.

It is not worse. My hon.
friend stated that yesterday I had said in this House that everything required by a poor man was exempt from taxation. I admit that, but I modified the statement by adding that almost everything that was a necessity of life was exempted from sales tax, and I repeat that statement.

What about
boots and Shoes?

And cotton goods and
clothing?
The sales tax on boots and shoes has been cut by 50 per cent.

It is still 2J
iper cent.

Yes, and that is why I
took the trouble to say "almost everything" that was a necessity.
Will the minister enumerate the articles required by the poor man, other than food, upon which he does not pay sales tax?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I must ask
both the minister and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) to keep to the subject under discussion.

I do not want to discuss
the matter further, since it was discussed in the House yesterday, but I think I am still in order when I say that whether or not the sales tax is reduced the poor man is getting the benefit of the reduction in income tax. The people who are exempt from taxation are those poor persons for whom an appeal was
Income War Tax Act

made for exemptions. The persons entirely-exempted from taxation under this act are those people having incomes of $3,000 and less. They are certainly not the opulent class, and not the multimillionaires.

They are not the poor
people, either.
I am willing to admit that they are not the poorest people; but they never paid any income tax.
They are in the class paying taxes.
Yes, and one of the most important taxes they pay is the customs duty, which my hon. friend has always advocated very Strongly in this House.

They pay it in order to
retain their employment in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are getting away
from the clause.

I certainly admire the way, Mr. Chairman, in which you are endeavouring to keep both the minister and those asking questions to the clause under discussion, and I will not refer again to the tariff or the sales tax. I will merely say that there is a real reduction in income tax in the present legislation. Everyone will admit that, and if there are any hon. members opposite Who claim that the reduction is too great, or who are in favour of having the income tax returned to its former figure, I should be very glad to hear from them. I think it is pretty nearly time, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs should devise some method of lightening the load on the working classes who are to-day paying these very heavy taxes. The government used to have an office in Toronto on Lombard street, in the old post office, where this tax was paid by the smaller man, often not by cheque but in cash. Unfortunately many of the working classes have no bank accounts to-day, under the economic laws of this government, and they cannot pay by cheque. I would like the indulgence of the committee for a moment while I make a few comments upon the remarks of the Minister of Customs and Excise in reference to my position. I conceive that there is a great difference between a public service utility company whose rates are subject to a public commission appointed for that purpose and an ordinary commercial company. Take for instance, a tramway company in Montreal. Its rates are governed by a public service commission and that commission in fixing rates must necessarily take into consideration the fact that a portion of the income of that company is diverted by means of the income tax into the federal treasury. Therefore the rates are fixed so as to allow of a certain dividend upon its shares or the capital stock invested, payment of interest upon its bonds, and also the approximate amount which is collected from the company under the income tax by the federal government. But that company in such a position necessarily takes from its patrons, or in a similar situation a lighting and power company would take from the users of its light and power, a higher rate in order to cover the income tax collected from it. That is the distinction between a public service utility company such as those we have in Quebec, and a public service utility commission such as the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission. Undter the

Ontario system the hydro-electric commission has not to provide in its rates for light and power that extra amount which is taken out of public utility companies in Quebec simply by reason of the fact that they are privately owned. I saw in the
Montreal papers the claim made that light and power was being sold there for less than it was in Ontario. How does the hon. gentle-iman explain that?

That may be so. In my
experience a privately-owned public utility company is operated and managed on so conservative a basis as compared with those publicly-owned that in many cases it is able to give a lower rate for its service than publicly-owned utility companies can. But my point is, in reply to the Minister of Customs, that a public utility company is in an entirely different position from an ordinary commercial company. The Minister of Customs said that because I made my argument in respect of the public utility company I thereby admitted that the ordinary commercial company raised the extra amount from its clientele and 'that its shareholders had no interest in the extra amount so raised. The ordinary commercial company is in open competition with the world; it is framed on the basis of a partnership; it is a limited liability company. The privately-owned commercial company is simply a partnership of its individual shareholders who have, it is true, [DOT]certain corporate rights and a certain limited liability, but its shareholders are entitled to the profits of the company in the proportion in which they own shares in it. The company is theirs; the profits are their property; they have no public service commission to whom they can go and ask that they be allowed a monopoly on the market and that as a monopoly they should impose higher prices for their commodities than ordinary market prices. Therefore they are in an entirely different position, and when you tax (first by 9 per cent the profits of the company you are taking that 9 per cent, or practically the equivalent of 9 per cent, from the pockets of the individual shareholders. When upon the remainder of the profits you charge the individual shareholders an income tax you are thereby imposing a double taxation upon those shareholders.

In this country, and I think in almost every other country which imposes an income tax, it is clearly recognized that double taxation should be avoided. It should be avoided (particularly in Canada where we need very large investments of money in corporate enterprises of that kind, privately-owned, in order to provide for the ordinary commercial -and industrial activities of the country. When you impose double taxation of that kind in Canada as against Canadian companies you put a premium upon the investment of Canadian funds in foreign enterprises abroad and you also put an obstacle in the way of securing the investment of foreign capital in commercial and industrial enterprises in this country. I do not think I need labour the point; I am presenting it to the government simply as a material and relevant consideration- that affects our whole commercial and industrial prosperity and that should therefore be carefully considered before such double taxation is imposed under these resolutions.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with this resolution I am going to offer a very brief criticism of what I deem to be the failure of the government to recognize what has always been regarded as a very sound principle in taxation, namely, that a given source of income should not be taxed a second time. I recognize that in collecting income tax there is naturally a desire to get the maximum. This is a very laudable desire on the part of the tax officials, but I still hold that if on the production of a certain amount of profit a company is taxed, it is unfair and unsound in principle to tax again that profit when it is paid out in the form of dividends. So I suggest to the minister the desirability of amending the resolution to eliminate this duplication of taxation.
I have in my hand a telegram dated April 23 last addressed to the Minister of Finance, and on behalf of those who sent it I want to say to the minister in charge of this resolution that the fact that it was not sent to him personally should not be taken amiss. It was addressed to the Minister of Finance, presumably under the impression that he would direct this legislation through the House. The telegram reads as folows:
1 At a meeting of citizens' committee representative city council, board of trade, Canadian Manufacturers' Association, B.C. division, Retail Merchants of Canada B.C. branch and Associated Property Owners of Vancouver to-day, I was instructed to make strongest opposition to provision in your budget of fifteenth instant for taxation of dividends both in hands of earning companies and again in hands of shareholders as dividends. This provision sufficiently onerous in any part of Canada to deter investment in new enterprises and particularly in new provinces such as British Columbia where introduction of new capital of supreme importance. Committee feel that proposed basis of taxation would be very serious and am instructed to urge upon you necessity of reconsidering proposed action in establishing dual taxation of company earnings if development of this province just beginning to give promise of considerable importance is not to be seriously retarded.
(Signed) A. E. Craddock,
Honorary Secretary.
I want to impress upon the minister the importance of the suggestion made in this telegram. It comes from a very representative group of citizens, and is not offered lightly or in a spirit of criticism, but with a desire to bring to his attention the possible serious effect of this taxation. They feel, and I feel, that if persisted in it will discourage the investment of capital in the development of our natural resources. I will localize this to a degree and speak for my own province. I suppose there is no province more dependent upon the investment of capital for the development of its natural resources, those of the mine, the forest and the sea principally, and in a lesser degree agriculture, and also in manufacturing, which is growing under the stimulus of the development of our resources. All of these activities are seriously affected, and we are therefore suggesting to the minister a reconsideration of this measure.
I have also before me a memorandum submitted to the Minister of Finance by Mr. Norman McLean, president of the Associated Property Owners of Vancouver. It deals with this same question, and I will read only a very brief section. It recommends that:
1.	The provincial income tax where levied be allowed as an exemption.
2.	Double taxation as will apply on dividends should be withhold, as all dividends are in the first instance subject to a tax paid by the company.

There is another point referred to there which only emphasizes my argument. We have a provincial income tax in British Columbia, as I understand they have in a number of other provinces, and that creates an additional difficulty; many concerns are now paying out a very considerable portion of their earnings in income tax. First there is the provincial income tax now reduced from 9 per cent to 8 per cent; then we have the federal company tax which is now 9 per cent,, formerly ten and one-half per cent, and in addition we have the tax upon the private individual on the same earnings. I am very seriously impressed with what I think will be in many instances the fatal results of this duplication. I will admit that there may perhaps be ways of getting around the tax by the reorganization of some concerns which may manage to escape this taxation, but it is not desirable to have legislation which some may escape but which others must observe. I think the object of all taxation should be to make it as clear and as simple in its operation as possible; in this instance we have multiplied taxation. I do not know whether the minister has so fixed a mind and an opinion upon the subject that we cannot appeal to him; I hope that is not the case.
I am sure there are many on the other side of the House who will quite agree with my view, imperfectly expressed as it is; I am giving it hurriedly and without much preparation. But the simple fact that we are taxing these incomes twice, first in the companies and then as they are distributed in the form of dividends or earnings, is in itself enough, I think, to warrant the government abandoning this particular portion of their budget proposals. I advance this suggestion in a spirit of good faith and with the desire of assisting in the study of this problem.

Before the minster replies I would like to say a word or ,wo on this point. I had a talk with the Minister of Finance on the subject; I did not know the Minister of Customs would have the matter in charge or I would have spoken to him as well. I am not interested in this question from the viewpoint of any individual or any particular company, but I do strongly support what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has said. I think it is going to hurt Canada if this resolution goes through in its present shape. In the first place, as has already been pointed out, it seems to me altogether contrary to the spirit of our taxation that the same money should be taxed twice; that is something which will hardly bear inspection. But passing along from that, I beg the minister 
to reconsider this resolution because it seems to me that it will be a hindrance to Canadian industry and Canadian investments.
This afternoon the remark was made that the dividends of a certain well established company should pay as much taxation as earned incomes. I do not think that is the point at all just now. I think there should be some inducement to people to invest their money in Canadian enterprises, and I ask the minister if he does not think that is a good principle to support. It should be made a little more profitable to put money into a Canadian enterprise than to put it into bonds. I know of a company which was started not long ago by ten men; that company may be a failure and the investors may lose their money, but if the company is successful, this resolution will make those men pay nine per cent in the first place as a company, and then each individual will have to pay an additional tax as well. People are going to think twice before investing money under these conditions. They will say, "If this company is a failure I will lose my money; if it is a success the government is going to take the bulk of the money; I had better put it into government bonds rather than risk it in any Canadian enterprise." Therefore I submit that the resolution as it is now framed will deter men with money to invest from putting it into new Canadian enterprises, and surely if there is one thing we need in this country it is to develop our resources. It is true that we are getting in a lot of outside money from the United States; we welcome it, and welcome even more the money coming from the Old Country, but it is much better that our enterprises should be controlled by ourselves so far as possible. So I submit to the minister that he should make some concession in regard to this resolution which will offer a certain amount of inducement to people to invest money in Canadian enterprises and Canadian stocks rather than in Canadian bonds.

I wish to support what has been said by previous speakers with regard to the principle of double taxation. In so doing I would like to refer briefly to what the minister said this afternoon in drawing a comparison between an earned income and an income drawn from dividends on money Invested in the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is very easy to draw a red herring across the trail by citing as an example a well known, well established public corporation, indicating that if a man has sufficient money in that enterprise to give him an income of $10,000 a year he should pay the same income tax

as a maa with an earned income. As a matter of fact he does pay the same; and at all events there are very few people in this country who have enough money invested in corporations such as the Canadian Pacific Railway to receive an income of $10,000 a year. They are not the people who are being hit by this legislation. But just at that point let me say that the Canadian Pacific Railway pays $2,000,000 in taxes direct to the federal government, and then the stockholders who put their money into the enterprise are taxed a second time. The great majority of the people who will be affected by this measure are those people in small industrial corporations of different kinds all over Canada. I know forty or fifty of them in my own riding, and the average aggregate income would not be over $10,000 or. perhaps $15,000 in any of these corporations.
When the minister spoke about earned income, he referred to the man who worked eighteen hours a day in order to secure that income. After all it is the man who pust his time and money into Canadian enterprise who works eighteen hours a day, and why should that man, receiving an increment of $10,000, pay $1,190 in taxes while the man who comes into Canada selling on commission goods produced in a foreign country and making an income of $10,000 only has to pay $290? Is there anything fair in that? That is exactly what happens; the man who earns $10,000 by selling goods produced in a foreign country will pay only $290 in taxes. The man who spends his own time and his iown money in the development of Canadian enterprise will pay $1,190; and so all along the line.
Another feature, and perhaps the most vicious feature in connection with this legislation, is the provision by which the increment that may be earned in a private corporation, notwithstanding the fact that it is not distributed or is not distributable-increment in the form of goods on the shelves . of a merchant or material in the plant of a manufacturer to be fabricated at some future time-is going to be subject not'only, in the *first place, to the corporation tax of 9 pel cent, but also to taxation upon dividends just the same as if it had been distributed, *although in all human probability in the majority of these cases the man who has that increment is paying interest to the bank in order to be able to carry his business along. Go through the whole of these provisions, examine just how they affect Canadian enterprise from one end of the country to the other, and, I will repeat what I said on a former 140U-240-i '

Is this practice which the

I understand that such companies have existed since 1917 with the full knowledge-I was almost going to say the approval-of the department. I think I am correct in saying that this condition has been well known to the commissioner and his staff for many years, almost since the inception of the act itself, but they have never raised any objection until now. What is the particular abuse at this moment that necessitates this legislation?
I think my hon. friend will admit it is an evil which it is worth while attempting to cure.
You have one income tax ca the profits of the company now.

If we were sure of getting the proper income tax it would not be so bad, but while it is true that a few of these personal corporations were established several years ago, I can assure my hon. friend there is no greater pastime for many able lawyers in Canada than to devise ways and means for their clients to evade payment of income tax.
Will not that always be so?

Yes, and for that reason as cracks are found in the walls of the structure, they must be continually repaired. That is why not only this year but in years to come, no matter what government may Joe in power, there will have to be amendments to the Income Tax Act to close the fissures that are being opened every year by the lawyers who devise new methods by which their clients may evade taxation.
Why does the hon. minister refer to their work as a "pastime"? Does he suggest that it is a recreation on the part of the lawyers?
It is a recreation for which the lawyer, however, never refuses to charge a fee.

The minister has stated that income of this character has been excaping taxation altogether. From what limited knowledge I have of this business, I submit to him that that is not quite correct, and that invariably one tax has been paid. The objection of course has been to pyramiding that taxation. Am I not right that invariably one tax of 10 per cent has been paid on income?
That is right.

My hon. friend is right to this extent, the company tax of 10 per cent, plus 5 per cent super tax or ten and one half per cent in all, has been collected from the company upon the profits declared by the company.
Earned by the company.

I mean declared by the company in its income tax return. That is the only tax which so far has been paid. In this particular instance we are dealing with shareholders whose revenue is very great. In the
Income War Tax Act

past they have been entitled to exemption only from payment of the normal tax, but they have been escaping payment of the surtax, that they should have paid to the Dominion government.

Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed in this connection to ask a question about section 4, which I overlooked at the time it was under discussion? It will save my bringing it up when the bill is before the House. Has the minister considered the fact that men with very large incomes are going to pay a great deal less under this legislation than they did before, even if the money is all in Canadian stocks? I have some figures from the department which perhaps I might read to him. In the case of a married man without children, if his income is $50,000, all from Canadian stocks, under the old system he paid $5,785.50; under the new he pays $8,380. True, he pays quite a little more. But if his income is $250,000-I am free to admit there are not many Canadians in receipt of such a large income-he ought to be able to pay a very substantial tax. His income is all from Canadian stocks. Under the old system he paid $112,885.50; under this resolution, which the government has brought in for the purpose of helping poor people, he pays only $86,340. In other words the very rich man with an income of $250,000 pays $26,500 les3 than he paid under the old law. I would ask if the minister is aware of that fact and if he considers it a reasonable arrangement.
Yes, we are aware that in every case the taxation has been reduced.
I have just cited a case where the man with $50,000 income pays more.
I mean in every case where the revenue exceeds $50,000.

I think it is
nearly $80,000.
.Mr. BOIVIN: For the purposes of agreement and argument we will say $80,000. In all cases where the revenue exceeds $80,000 there is a reduction. It was necessary to establish a sliding scale in order to reach a fair basis of payment for the small income, the moderate income, the larger income and the very large income, and we thought the limit of that scale should be 50 per cent. Under the old law, as my hon. friend knows, some people were called upon to pay as much as 66 per cent and more of their revenue to the government. We felt that any man who invests his money in Canada and pays at least half of what he makes to the Dom-

inion government is contributing fairly generously his share of taxation, and we thought it should no longer be necessary to take away from any man more than half of his income. At present we do not happen to have in Canada anyone with an income of $1,000,000, and the income would have to reach that amount before the taxation would be the full 50 per cent.

Section agreed to.
On section 13.

This amendment ensures
that the shareholders of corporations will pay income tax upon the profits of the corporation as and when they get control of such profits. Under the provisions of the Income War Tax Act shareholders of a corporation, in contrast with members of a partnership, are not taxed upon the profits of the business at the time the profits are earned. Taxation is deferred until the profits become the property of the shareholders or until something is done'that renders the profits not available for distribution to the shareholders. The policy under our Canadian act is to defer taxation of corporation profits so long as they remain available for dsitribution, which is to say so long as there is prospect of a tax being imposed upon the shareholder at some future time. As soon as the profits are capitalized they cease to be available for distribution, and it seems only right and proper that the profits should be taxed when placed beyond the possibility of distribution.
But in that case you have already collected 10^ per cent from the corporation, and you are simply imposing a second tax on the same profits.

We are simply endeavouring there to obtain the surtax and supertax which the shareholder would have paid had he received the dividend in another form. We do not desire to tax the dividend again; we are quite willing to give the exemption from the normal tax to which the shareholder is entitled, but we do claim that when the profits are taken out in enormous slices the shareholders should be called upon to pay at least the surtax and supertax which they would have paid had they withdrawn their dividends in the ordinary way.

That is all very well, but you take your supertax in the form of an increased normal tax at the beginning. That is why the tax is increased to 10 per cent instead of 4 per cent, and that is why you had no supertax on the profits of a corpora-

Income War Tax Act
tion. Now you want to take the supertax in the 10 per cent and another supertax on the distribution of the profits as well. That is simply double taxation.

This question of double
taxation, as my hon. friend knows, was thoroughly discussed in connection with clause 4 and we came very close to an agreement then. There are certain classes of corporations which we hope to be able to deal with in a manner satisfactory to everyone. In small corporations this clause would never apply, because the corporation has always the right of exercising its option to be treated as a partnership and not as a corporation.
This is retroactive?
Yes, retroactive as to profits earned.
Is that usual?
That is one of the reasons why I referred in my remarks a moment ago to the surtax and supertax; this is a retroactive clause.	,

Section agreed to.
On section 14.

In connection with this resolution there was one thing which a great many hon. gentlemen opposite were in favour of when I was Minister of Finance, that is, the question of members of parliament having their election expenses deducted from their returns. I wonder what the present ideas of hon. gentlemen opposite are. I know they were almost unanimously in favour of it at that time, and I think my friend the minister favoured it also. What does he think now?
We thought it would be better to follow the line of conduct laid down by our predecessors.
If you would only stick to that more often you would do better.

I think our predecessors made a mistake, however, when they did not allow members of parliament to deduct from their indemnity a reasonable amount to pay for living expenses while in Ottawa. I would say that the same rule would apply to electoral expenses-
That is a capital investment.

-although I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that that is a capital investment.
If each member paid the same amount to be elected, or if each member only paid the amount absolutely necessary for him to be elected, or if we could average that amount, it might be possible and advisable to make some allowance when it comes to the payment of income tax. I will repeat that I think it would be absolutely fair to allow members of parliament to deduct from their indemnity a just and reasonable amount for board and living expenses while they are in the capital attending to their parliamentary duties. It is an expense which they are absolutely obliged to make, but my good friends opposite were generous enough to make a gift of this to the Canadian people. They wanted to be magnanimous, and we want to follow their example and be just as generous as they are.

Section agreed to.
On section 15.

This is a clause concerning which there has been some discussion; some claim it is not necessary at all while others say it clarifies the act. It merely adds that the provisions of paragraph (d) concerning taxes and supertaxes will not apply.

I just want to ask the minister one further question. What has been done in connection with that debatable question where you have a man employed at a stated salary whose tax is paid by his employer? There has been more or less soreness over that. I understand the department in the past have come to the conclusion that that money belonged to the employee and should be added to his gross income for the purposes of taxation. On the other hand it is urged very strongly that where any employer voluntarily pays to the Receiver General the whole or any part of the income tax on the salary or wages of the employee, that amount shall not be treated as part of the income of the employee for the purpose of income tax.

My impression is that it would be absolutely unfair to consider that the tax paid for an employee should not form part of his income. Two corporations side by side, paying absolutely the same salary to their employees, make out their returns to the Dominion government showing, for instance, that they each have a superintendent drawing 14,000 or $5,000 a year. One company would pay the tax while the other would not, so one man would have his $4,000 net while the other would be obliged to pay his $20
Income War Tax Act

to the government. That would be unfair and unjust, because in reality one man would have $4,000 a year while the net salary of the other would only be $3,980.
Will the language be sufficiently clear to show that this will be made retroactive?
How far would you go back?

I would go back to the inception of the Income War Tax Act. I would tax all those dividends. There is no desire on the part of the government to take these accumulative profits and consider them to be profits of this year. That would be absolutely unfair and unjust. The tax upon them would be almost 50 per cent.
It would be more-

Applying the present law the tax upon them would be almost 50 per cent, whereas if they had been distributed normally year by year the tax might have been very much less. There is no intention of being too severe, but it would be possible to allow those who have accumulated these profits during the last five years-the first companies were formed five years ago-a term of five years within which to distribute those profits. They could be distributed as they like in that period of five years, but if they were not distributed at the end of five years, then they could be taxed as the profits of that year.
My point was simply as to the language being express enough.
It will be made express enough in the bill.

I rise merely to ask a question. I know the Income Tax branch has two, if not more, very shrewd and competent solicitors, but in view of the question

that has been raised previously, has the minister thb opinion of the Justice department that these retroactive provisions are not ultra vires? Just in that connection let me point out this the point was raised by the hen. member for Vancouver-Burrard-if you could tax income past and gone for the year 1925, you could pass a law to tax it for the year 1825. I am merely asking whether an opinion has been obtained.

The opinion of the solicitors in our own department and the opinion of the Department of Justice was obtained in the matter. I am not sure whether the final opinion from the Department of Justice, has been received, but at least one memorandum from that department has reached us. I want to say to my bon. friend that he is not quite fair. I know that he does -not want to be unfair to the government or to the legislation, but I think he is unfair when he says that we are indiscriminately reaching back and taxing income, and that because we do it for the past five years we might as well do it for the last hundred years. That is not the intention of the government. The proper thing for the government to do is to reach back and tax that income which would have paid taxes to the Dominion government but did ndt do so. The object of the amendment is to try to reach that income, to bring the tax into the public treasury, and ward against such evasions of payment in the future. When I say evasions of payment, I want to be fair to those persons who formed these corporations sole. I do not want to say they are tax dodgers; I do not want to apply any damaging epithet to them.

You referred
to them as fake companies the other day.

Oh no, I did not. The
other day I referred to fake companies in connection with the customs tariff-to those companies which were importing automobiles and getting excessive discounts for importing them. I never referred to these corporations as fake companies. They were formed legally under the Companies Act, and it was up to the government so to frame its legislation as to be able to collect the tax. They were within the law, and when a man is within the law he cannot be blamed. On the other hand, a man can remain within the law and evade the tax that a former government intended to impose upon him. We want to reach back and collect those taxes; that is all.

I cannot let go unchallenged the minister's statement that I was not fair. I was asking purely an academic question as to the legality of this legislation- nothing else. It did not enter my mind to criticize the action of the government if they were warranted in law in taking the action which they propose to take. I certainly had no idea other than merely to obtain an answer to the question whether an opinion had been obtained, because frankly I do not think this is within the competency of this parliament to enact.

We are so advised. If I
misunderstood my hon. friend or one of his references, and said anything which I should not have said, I hasten to apologize.

With reference to the
observations made by the minister as to the purposes for which these holding companies were formed, I think it is only fair to him to say that in the smaller provinces these companies were not formed with the express purpose of evading the supertax, but having regard to the lack of reciprocity between the provinces with respect to succession duties, most if not all of them were primarily formed for the purpose of evading the payment of double succession duties to the various provinces on securities such as the stock of companies having their head office in a province other than that in which the company was domiciled.
